lecture_summary: Circular-motion dynamics using free-body diagrams and vertical/inward-radial axes. The lecture applies ΣFy = 0 and ΣFr = mv²/r to a car on a flat curve, frictionless and frictional banked curves, and a conical pendulum, emphasizing that “centripetal force” is the net inward effect of real forces—not an additional force.

videos.title: Physics - What Is a Centripetal Force?
videos.reason: Establishes the lecture’s central conceptual rule: centripetal force is the inward net force, which real forces such as tension, static friction, or gravity can supply.

videos.title: Static Friction, Centripetal Force, Circular Motion, Car Rounding Curve & Rotor Ride Physics Problem
videos.reason: Direct match for the flat-curve example: draw the force picture, recognize static friction as the radial force, and determine the maximum speed or required friction before slipping.

videos.title: Banked turn Physics Problems
videos.reason: Best direct match for resolving the normal force on a frictionless banked curve and finding the design speed, then extending the analysis to minimum and maximum non-sliding speeds with friction.

videos.title: Tetherball Physics Problem - Calculate Tension Force
videos.reason: Closest playlist equivalent to the conical pendulum: the vertical tension component balances weight while the horizontal component supplies the inward radial force.

coverage_gaps: No playlist entry explicitly names the conical pendulum; the tetherball problem is a strong physical analog, but its description does not guarantee coverage of conical-pendulum geometry such as r = L sin θ.

The banked-turn entry covers limiting speeds, but its description does not explicitly guarantee the lecture’s detailed explanation of why static friction reverses direction above versus below the frictionless design speed.
The playlist metadata does not guarantee reproduction of the lecture’s exact numerical examples, symbolic maximum-speed formula for a frictional bank, or repeated demonstrations that mass cancels.
